audit:admin / merchant / dev console.summary:
VERDICT: The OOM defences in this subsystem exist because the admin GETs copy raw rows from the database into Python and aggregate them there. The gate, the RSS shed, gc/malloc_trim after each burst, three layers of single-flight, the HEAVY and ADMIN_IO pools, and the row caps with their truncated flags all treat that symptom. Every aggregate involved is either a COUNT/SUM/AVG/GROUP BY that Postgres can return as about 2KB of JSONB, or a value derived from a 10-minute parking bucket that never changes after it is written. Move the first kind into SQL RPCs and precompute the second kind when each bucket is written, and each heavy admin GET moves kilobytes instead of megabytes. After that, about 700 lines of patch code can be deleted (memory_guard gate/shed/trim, admin_coalesce, the per-router and per-service in-flight maps, the estimate timeouts, the HEAVY pool, _fetch_capped and its caps).

HEAVY GET INVENTORY (rows pulled -> work done; sizes measured locally on synthetic data at the caps):
1. GET /admin/model-trust (admin.py:544-735). Pulls up to 10k recommendations (JSON-path slim select), up to 10k outcomes, up to 20k congestion_logs and all ~1,689 facilities. That is about 43 OFFSET pages. Python then does funnel, guardrail and coverage loops plus a sort. Size: 9.96MB on the wire, 25.8MB of Python heap.
2. GET /admin/metrics (admin.py:433-471). Up to 5k recommendations and up to 5k feedback rows, sent raw to the browser. The browser computes acceptance rate and DAU (dashboard/page.tsx:510-533). Size: 0.86MB.
3. GET /admin/metrics/trend (admin.py:773-845). Up to 20k logs and up to 5k recommendations, grouped by KST day in Python. Size: 2.18MB, 7.3MB heap.
4. GET /admin/impact (admin.py:942-1000). Up to 5k accepted recommendations with the score_breakdown jsonb, summed in Python. Size: 3.44MB, 9.3MB peak.
5. GET /admin/dashboard/today (admin.py:1396-1490). Up to 12k logs joined to facilities, up to 5k rows for the previous day, and, when today has no logs (the common case), a 5k-timestamp scan plus a fallback day of up to 12k+5k rows. On top of that it runs the estimated-day recompute for today and yesterday (288 snapshots × 1,689 facilities, 246ms CPU per day). The aggregation and a 2.85MB JSON encode run on the event loop.
6. GET /admin/dashboard/briefing. Runs #5 and #4 again, then a 3s LLM call, while holding a gate slot.
7. GET /admin/reports/estimated. 30 days of embedded snapshots (about 4,320 parents and 17k lot rows) plus facilities and forecasts; 280ms CPU plus about 2.5s of DB time.
8. GET /admin/area-demand-reliability. Up to 1,008 bucket rows, 2 boundary rows and the latest snapshot's lots. The dashboard polls it every 60s and GitHub Actions calls it hourly.
9. GET /admin/area-demand-forecast-quality. A 56-day point RPC plus a backtest.
10. GET /admin/safety/status. All facilities plus an RPC with 1,682 UUIDs, then 2 sklearn predictions per logged facility on the event loop. The page polls every 30s.
11. GET /admin/engine-validation/seoul/summary. 14 days of Seoul rows with fcst JSON (about 10k rows once collection runs; the table is empty today).
12. GET /admin/engine-validation/seoul/alternatives. 7 days × 3 areas (about 3k rows) read just to get the latest row per area.
13. GET /admin/engine-validation/seoul/calibration. 28 days of Seoul rows, plus 4,032 Gyeongju parent rows and 21 batches of `in_` lot reads. The lot reads are redundant: the snapshot row already stores the same occupancy.
14. GET /preference-stats/categories. Scans every users row, including anonymous ones.
15. GET /merchant/stats. Three `.limit(5000)` reads that PostgREST silently caps at 1000 rows, used only for counts.
16. GET /impact/summary. All of a user's recommendations with score_breakdown.
17. GET /dev/users. A full GoTrue list_users scan (all anonymous users included) on each 120s cache miss.

TARGET DESIGN, in four tiers:
(a) In-database aggregation for anything that is a count, sum, average or group-by. Each is an RPC that returns a single JSONB value, granted to service_role only. The repo already does this with area_demand_points_near, which also sidesteps PostgREST's silent 1000-row cap. Use RPCs rather than PostgREST's built-in aggregate functions: PostgREST ships with those disabled by default (https://docs.postgrest.org/en/v14/references/api/aggregate_functions.html, https://supabase.com/blog/postgrest-aggregate-functions).
(b) Rollups computed when data is written, for the parking-derived estimates. The input is about 4 lot occupancies per 10-minute bucket. Computing one bucket's estimate costs 1.7ms, so do it once in the collector instead of re-deriving 288 or 4,320 buckets on every read.
(c) Scheduled precompute for backtests, the calibration curve and the Seoul validation metrics, stored as one row each. pg_cron is already used here. Materialized views are another option, but REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-refreshmaterializedview.html, https://supabase.com/blog/supabase-cron).
(d) A lookup table for the Ridge-on-one-hot model. It has 672 input combinations; the table matched per-row predictions exactly (0 mismatches) and a lookup takes 0.08µs versus 0.355ms per sklearn call.

PREREQUISITE: CI has no real Postgres. The migration tests only check SQL text, so a parity harness is needed before any of this can ship without regressions.

SEQUENCE: CI Postgres harness and indexes, then the predict lookup table, then the RPCs endpoint by endpoint (each keeps a Python fallback for one release, following the pattern at infrastructures.py:313-336), then the write-time estimate rollups, then delete the gate, coalescing and pools.

The response shapes (including `truncated` and the legacy changePercent key) and the handler docstrings must stay unchanged. The OpenAPI snapshot locks path, parameters and description; admin response schemas are `{}` in it.

findings.title: Admin aggregate GETs page raw rows into Python — replace with JSONB-returning SQL RPCs (model-trust, metrics, metrics/trend, impact, dashboard/today)
findings.evidence: admin.py:62-99 `_fetch_capped` loops PostgREST `.range()` (LIMIT/OFFSET) pages up to per-endpoint caps (admin.py:430,476-478,757-759,939,1017-1026). model-trust admin.py:553-600 gathers model_registry + recommendations source='spot' ≤10,000 (slim JSON-path select 485-541 with full-snapshot fallback) + recommendation_outcomes ≤10,000 + congestion_logs ≤20,000 + fetch_all_rows(facilities) then loops 605-735 (scoring_modes, top3, closed, walk violations, ungrounded, outcome join, coverage sets, gaps sort). metrics/trend 780-845 buckets ≤20k logs + ≤5k recs by KST day in Python (810-842, on the event loop). impact 960-1000 sums score_breakdown over ≤5k accepted recs. dashboard/today 1087-1150 pulls ≤12k joined logs + ≤5k prev-day levels (+5k timestamp scan + fallback 12k/5k when today is empty — admin.py:1478-1486). All listed in memory_guard.py:76-88 and wrapped in @coalesced_admin_view (admin.py:434,545,774,943,1397).
findings.cost: Measured locally (synthetic rows at caps, json.loads under tracemalloc; see scratchpad bench_rows.py): model-trust 9.96MB wire → 25.8MB Python heap (+ httpx bytes/str transient ≈2-3× wire) and ~43 page round trips; dashboard/today 2.87MB → 10.7MB; metrics/trend 2.18MB → 7.3MB; impact 3.44MB → 5.9MB (peak 9.3MB); metrics 0.86MB → 3.2MB. One dashboard open = sum of 7 panels ≈ 50-60MB heap + transient buffers — exactly the '7 heavy GETs summed' OOM described in memory_guard.py:3-9 (8 OOM restarts). Every OFFSET page re-scans; recommendations has no created_at index (only user_id, RESET_AND_SETUP.sql:151-152) so each of up to 10 pages is a seq-scan + sort. At today's volumes (congestion_logs mostly seed, simulate-peak adds ~1,660 rows per press, admin.py:747-751) the dominant cost is round trips, but it grows linearly with users/demo presses. SQL equivalent returns ~1-3KB.
findings.proposal: New migration with service_role-only RPCs each returning ONE jsonb (precedent: area_demand_points_near returns single JSONB to dodge the 1000-row cap, RESET_AND_SETUP.sql ~3630-3640): (1) admin_reco_feedback_summary(p_since, p_day_start, p_day_end) → per-KST-day {total, accepted} for source<>'browse' + count(*)/count(distinct user_id) of user_feedback in the day; (2) admin_daily_trend(p_since) → GROUP BY (timestamp AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Seoul')::date → avg(congestion_level), count; (3) admin_impact(p_since) → count, sum(greatest(0,(sb->>'original_wait_time')::float8-(sb->>'wait_time')::float8)) FILTER(both present), count measured, sum(greatest(0,(sb->>'incentive_relief')::float8))*15 FILTER(legacy); (4) admin_model_trust(p_since) → funnel via LEFT JOIN outcomes, guardrail counts via jsonb paths, scoring_mode GROUP BY, by_source/by_tier GROUP BY, active facility count, covered-active count, facility_gaps = first 20 active facilities NOT EXISTS trusted log ORDER BY type,name; (5) admin_congestion_day(p_start,p_end) (see dashboard finding) + admin_latest_aggregatable_day(p_min_samples) = GROUP BY KST date HAVING count>=5 ORDER BY 1 DESC LIMIT 1. Handlers become 1 RPC call + small dict assembly; keep rounding (_js_round half-up, admin.py:1029-1033) in Python on the returned aggregates; keep `truncated` keys (always false). Keep the current Python aggregators as test oracles only.
findings.makes_unnecessary: _fetch_capped + all caps/truncation warnings (admin.py:44-99 and cap constants); _TRUST_REC_SELECT/_trust_snapshot/_fetch_trust_recommendations slim+fallback (485-541); _recent_congestion_timestamps/_pick_fallback_day Python scan (1120-1183); run_admin_io/ADMIN_IO pool usage in admin.py (executors.py:40,92-94); these paths in _HEAVY_ADMIN_PATHS; coalesce decorators on them; tests test_admin_row_cap.py and test_admin_model_trust_slim_select.py (rewrite against an RPC fake).
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Medium. SQL must reproduce the subtle semantics: KST day edges, null sentinel vs 0.0, legacy changePercent=0.0 + changePercentOrNull, same-timestamp tie handling. Migrations are applied by hand in the SQL Editor (HANDOVER.md:149-154), so each handler should fall back to the current Python path on PGRST202 'function not found' for one release (pattern: infrastructures.py:313-336). model-trust's fresh_rate/fresh_trusted_measured_rate compare the snapshot timestamp to the dashboard's `now` (admin.py:639-653, congestion_evidence.py:60-67, 30-minute window), not to the recommendation's created_at, so for a 30-day window they tend toward 0. A port to SQL must either keep that (bit-parity) or fix it, and fixing it changes displayed numbers (PM decision, check DEMO_SCENARIO/JUDGE_QA). Docstrings are in the OpenAPI snapshot; don't edit them.

findings.title: dashboard/today aggregates and JSON-encodes a facility×24 heatmap on the event loop (up to 2.85MB, ~0.6s desktop)
findings.evidence: admin.py:1466 `today = _aggregate_congestion_day(logs, y_logs)` runs inline in the async handler (also admin.py:1337 in the fallback). The heatmap emits 24 cells for every facility that has any log (admin.py:1248-1273). The response goes through FastAPI jsonable_encoder. The web view paginates by type and calls `heatmapData.find` per cell (DashboardCharts.tsx:273-298), and the predicted view only uses the top 12 per type (adminPredictedView.ts:45 HEATMAP_PLACE_CAP=12). Briefing and the report page (report/page.tsx:154) call the same endpoint.
findings.cost: Measured locally with the real function on 12k logs over 1,700 facilities (the simulate-peak shape): aggregation 410ms, 40,776 heatmap cells, jsonable_encoder 157ms, JSONResponse render 25ms, body 2.85MB. That is about 0.6s of event-loop time per call on a fast desktop, several times more on Render's 0.5 CPU. During that stall /health (5s restart budget, main.py:268-271) and every tourist request wait. A columnar encoding of the same heatmap is 263KB.
findings.proposal: Compute the heatmap inside admin_congestion_day in SQL: avg(level) per (facility, KST hour) only for the top-N facilities per type (N=12, ranked by samples or peak), the six anomaly peaks (DISTINCT ON facility ORDER BY level DESC LIMIT 6), avg, anomaly count, source composition, and previous-day avg/count, all in one jsonb. Python then only reshapes at most 4×12×24 cells in the existing flat format, so the web contract is unchanged; a columnar form can be added later as additive keys. Serialize small responses directly (Response(bytes)). Past days are immutable, so the fallback-day result can be stored in the same rollup table as the estimates (next finding) and served as pre-serialized bytes.
findings.makes_unnecessary: The Python heatmap, peak and composition loops; _joined_facility and per-row _kst_hour/_parse_utc (admin.py:1071-1084); the 12k/5k caps; the O(n²) `find` cost in the client.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low-medium. Capping heatmap rows changes what the admin sees after simulate-peak (not used in the demo per DEMO_SCENARIO.md:136-137), so check with the PM against DEMO_SCENARIO/JUDGE_QA before shipping. Interim single-line mitigation: move the aggregation into asyncio.to_thread.

findings.title: safety/status runs 2 sklearn predictions per facility on the event loop every 30s; a 672-entry lookup table makes them free
findings.evidence: safety.py:140-188 loops over facilities and calls _predict_next_hour synchronously (safety.py:63-73 → predict_congestion twice). predict_service.py:208-218 does encoder.transform + model.predict per call. The model is Ridge on one-hot (type, hour, dow) (scripts/train.py:68-72), so the whole input domain is 4×24×7=672 points. Facilities are refetched on every call (safety.py:76-80, 2 anon pages), then latest_congestion_for_facilities gets 1,682 UUIDs in the POST body (infrastructures.py:308-318). The page auto-refreshes every 30s (safety/page.tsx:21,244). Not coalesced; on the heavy-gate list (memory_guard.py:86). merchant_briefing_service.py:134-145 makes 8 more predict calls through to_thread per briefing.
findings.cost: Measured: sklearn predict is 0.355ms per call, so 3,320 calls (all facilities logged) = 1.18s of event-loop blocking locally, several seconds on 0.5 CPU, repeated every 30s while the safety page is open. Building an exact lookup table (672 per-row predicts) takes 237ms once per model load with 0 mismatches; batch predict differs by at most 5.6e-17; a lookup takes 0.08µs.
findings.proposal: (a) In predict_service, when a model snapshot is activated, build `table[(norm_type, hour, dow)] -> float | None` with per-row predict (bit-exact), store it on the snapshot, and make predict_congestion a dict lookup. That removes sklearn from every request path (safety, merchant briefing, courses, /predict). (b) Replace the facility fetch plus UUID-list RPC with one `safety_latest_levels()` SQL function (DISTINCT ON congestion_logs JOIN active facilities, same source/tier filters) returning only facilities that have logs, with name/type/lat/lng. The 150m zone roll-up (round(lat,3), round(lng,3)) can be a GROUP BY in the same function. (c) Return an ETag = max(log id/timestamp) + thresholds so the 30s polls get a 304 when nothing changed.
findings.makes_unnecessary: The sklearn call overhead everywhere; the to_thread wrappers around predict in merchant_briefing_service; the full-facility refetch in safety; safety's entry in the heavy gate.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low. The table must be swapped atomically with the model snapshot (the model manager polls every 5 minutes), and unknown categories must keep returning None. Parity is provable with a test that compares all 672 keys.

findings.title: Parking-derived estimate aggregates are re-derived from raw buckets on every read — precompute a per-bucket rollup when the 10-minute bucket is written
findings.evidence: congestion_estimator_service.py:622-639 `_estimated_day_sync` loads the day's snapshots and lots (446-470), all facilities (374-388), forecasts and calibration, and runs estimate_facilities for every snapshot × 1,689 facilities (276-288). with_prev=True recomputes yesterday too (629-634). Today's result is cached for only 5 minutes (643-645). estimated_report_service.py:446-456 and 532-560 load 30 days of embedded snapshots (about 4,320 parents and 17k lot rows) and recompute. The input per bucket is about 4 lot occupancies (parking_derived_congestion_service.py:138).
findings.cost: Measured locally with the real functions: the day aggregate costs 246ms CPU (144 snapshots × 1,689 facilities) and runs twice per call (today + yesterday), which is the '콜드 1~3초' on 0.5 CPU cited at admin.py:1350. The 30-day report costs 280ms CPU plus about 2.5s of DB (estimated_report_service.py:17). Computing one bucket's estimate_facilities costs 1.7ms, so nearly all read-time CPU re-derives values that are fixed once the bucket exists.
findings.proposal: In the 10-minute collect path (pg_cron → POST /area-demand/snapshots/collect → record_area_demand_snapshot), after storing the snapshot, compute that bucket once with the existing pure functions and upsert `estimated_bucket_rollups`: bucket_at PK, kst_date, calibration_version, forecast_date_version, by_type jsonb {type: [sum, count, anomalies]}, place_levels jsonb {facility_id: level} for representative places, covered_count, lot_count, observed_at. That is about 1KB per row, 144 rows per day. Today's aggregate is then a fold over ≤144 rows (store sums and counts, never averages). The 30-day series is a GROUP BY kst_date over ≤4,320 rows, keeping the minute%30 sampling filter so output stays byte-identical. Finished past days go into `estimated_day_rollups` as pre-serialized JSON. Add a backfill job for history, and recompute a date's rows when that date's tourism forecasts arrive late or the calibration version changes. Calibration is currently identity because the Seoul table has 0 rows (HANDOVER.md:50).
findings.makes_unnecessary: estimated_report_service caches, _lock and _facility_cache (370-388, 475-507); congestion_estimator_service _day_cache, _day_inflight and _compute_day (643-702); admin _estimate_inflight and _report_estimate_inflight with their 12s/10s timeouts and the 'timeout' degraded responses (admin.py:861-924, 1354-1393); the HEAVY pool (executors.py:39, 87-89); the aggregate_estimated_days geometry-cache machinery (keep it as a test oracle).
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Medium. Equivalence depends on storing sums and counts, keeping per-bucket place levels for the per-hour heatmap, and fixing representative places using that date's forecasts. The current rule 'apply the current calibration curve to the whole day' (congestion_estimator_service.py:263-264) becomes 'curve version at write time', so the version must be recorded and changes must trigger a recompute. The collector gains about 2ms of CPU per bucket and must not fail the snapshot insert if the rollup fails: write the rollup best-effort and let the reader recompute missing buckets.

findings.title: The heavy-admin gate's side effects: full gc + malloc_trim after every lone poll, gate slots held through LLM calls and 12s waits, and an RSS-shed 503 that trips the machine monitor
findings.evidence: memory_guard.py:237-272 runs release_memory (gc.collect + malloc_trim) whenever _pending hits 0 after a success, so every isolated poll triggers it: AreaDemandReliabilityPanel.tsx:64 (60s), safety/page.tsx:244 (30s), and the hourly area-demand-alert. The slot is held for the whole handler, including briefing's LLM call (admin.py:1532-1536; LLM_TIMEOUT 3s, config.py:121) and up-to-12s estimate waits, with HEAVY_ADMIN_CONCURRENCY=2 (memory_guard.py:50). The dashboard's 7 panels queue behind the 25s web timeout (admin-api.ts:30) and withColdStartRetry resubmits them (dashboard/page.tsx:453-466). The RSS shed returns 503 (memory_guard.py:283-294); area-demand-alert.yml:54-61 retries and then fails, and HANDOVER.md:216 records a 503-driven false alarm. The Dockerfile already fixes the mmap/trim thresholds at 128KB (Dockerfile:22-26).
findings.cost: A full gc on a synthetic warm-like heap (630k tracked objects) takes 58-60ms with the GIL held on a desktop. Running it via to_thread does not release the GIL, so on 0.5 CPU it means hundreds of milliseconds of event-loop stall every 30-60s while an admin page is open. The gate itself is about 250 lines of ASGI code sitting ahead of auth on every request.
findings.proposal: Once the aggregate, dashboard, safety and estimate findings land, admin GETs move kilobytes. Then delete HeavyAdminGateMiddleware and its registration (main.py:223-225) and keep release_memory only for the tourist warmup (warmup.py:187) until the walking-graph and area-demand subsystems shrink. Point the area-demand-alert workflow at a DB-side check (a service_role RPC over area_demand_snapshots; the Supabase secrets are already in Actions, HANDOVER.md:94-96) so the monitor no longer depends on the API's cold starts or shedding. Interim, if deletion has to wait: drop reliability and safety from _HEAVY_ADMIN_PATHS, and skip the burst trim for requests that never touched the gate's memory budget.
findings.makes_unnecessary: memory_guard.py gate, _LoopBoundSemaphore, _replay_first, preflight/shed, _send_busy and the HEAVY_ADMIN_* env knobs (roughly lines 48-100 and 163-323); the gate tests in tests/core/test_memory_guard.py; the Render env vars HEAVY_ADMIN_TRIM_RSS_MB/SHED_RSS_MB.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: High if done too early: removing the gate before the aggregate and estimate work lands reopens the 09-25 OOM. Strictly sequence it last, and watch Render RSS for one admin session after each step.

findings.title: Three stacked single-flight/cache layers for the same estimate computations, plus a coalescer coupled to the ASGI middleware
findings.evidence: dashboard/today: the @coalesced_admin_view decorator (admin.py:1397), then the router's _estimate_inflight + shield + 12s wait_for (admin.py:1357-1393), then the service's _day_inflight + shield + _day_cache (congestion_estimator_service.py:643-702). reports/estimated: the decorator (admin.py:884), then _report_estimate_inflight (863-924), then the service _lock + _day_cache + _basis_cache (estimated_report_service.py:475-610). Invalidating on admin writes lives in the ASGI middleware (memory_guard.py:296-309 → admin_coalesce.invalidate, admin_coalesce.py:79-82). Briefing calls the coalesced handlers directly (admin.py:1532-1535) and briefing_service has its own 12-minute cache (briefing_service.py:39-48). Every joiner gets copy.deepcopy of the result (admin_coalesce.py:59).
findings.cost: About 250 lines of concurrency code, each layer with its own loop-affinity checks and exception-retrieval callbacks. In the worst case the 2.85MB dashboard/today result is deep-copied once per joiner. Freshness gets reasoned about in three places.
findings.proposal: With reads reduced to one RPC and estimates reduced to rollup reads, delete admin_coalesce.py and both router in-flight maps. Admin writes are then visible immediately because the DB is the only state, with no generation counter to bump. If coalescing is ever needed again, add one generic keyed singleflight utility in core, not one per layer.
findings.makes_unnecessary: admin_coalesce.py (89 lines) and its 11 decorator sites (admin.py, area_demand_admin.py:30,51, engine_validation_admin.py:153,284, engine_validation_calibration.py:43); memory_guard._admin_write; tests/core/test_admin_coalesce.py.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low once the RPC and rollup work lands. Before that, removing coalescing doubles concurrent heavy work.

findings.title: Calibration: a threading.Lock held across a network read on the tourist path, and a calibration report that re-reads lot rows the snapshot row already sums
findings.evidence: congestion_calibration_service.py:650-672 `active_calibration` holds _cache_lock while _build_state runs fetch_all_rows over 28 days of Seoul rows (499-521). It is called from the tourist path current_estimates → _compute_current (congestion_estimator_service.py:566-570) and from the admin day/report paths. The failure TTL is 600s, and the table currently has 0 rows, so the query repeats every 10 minutes. build_report (701-742) calls _load_gyeongju_levels (524-572): 4,032 parent rows plus 21 `in_` batches of 200 UUIDs of lot rows, only to compute Σ(total-available)/Σtotal per bucket. record_area_demand_snapshot already stores exactly those sums on the snapshot row (RESET_AND_SETUP.sql:2243-2244), and area_demand_snapshots.occupancy is a generated column equal to that ratio (RESET_AND_SETUP.sql:1818-1822).
findings.cost: Any thread that needs calibration while Supabase is slow blocks in a pool slot; the default pool of 16 is shared with DNS (main.py:23-39). The calibration report makes 21+ round trips and reads about 16k lot rows that are redundant.
findings.proposal: Treat calibration as a derived artifact. A scheduled job (hourly pg_cron → service endpoint, or piggy-backed on the 10-minute Seoul collect) fits the curve and writes a single `congestion_calibration_state` row (knots, applied, basis, version, fitted_at). Readers load that row, or an in-process copy refreshed when the version changes, and never take a lock around I/O. For the Gyeongju hour shape, select bucket_at and occupancy from area_demand_snapshots, or GROUP BY KST hour and weekend in SQL, with zero lot reads.
findings.makes_unnecessary: The lock-around-I/O and the TTL cache in active_calibration; the lot-batch loop in _load_gyeongju_levels; per-request curve fitting in build_report (the report shows the stored fit plus quality metrics).
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low. Occupancy parity: the DB computes 1 - Σa/Σt and Python computes Σ(t-a)/Σt, which can differ by 1 ulp before clamping and rounding; the hour_shape outputs are rounded, so assert with a tolerance.

findings.title: No real-Postgres parity harness in CI — prerequisite for moving any aggregate into SQL safely
findings.evidence: tests/migrations/*.py only assert SQL text (for example test_area_demand_snapshot_migration.py:26-34). No psycopg or Postgres anywhere in tests. The existing SQL port (area_demand_points_near) depends on a hand-mirrored Python version plus comments (RESET_AND_SETUP.sql:3610-3630). Migrations are applied remotely by hand (HANDOVER.md:149-154), and there is no staging (HANDOVER.md:112).
findings.cost: Every SQL RPC proposed here would ship unexecuted until production. A wrong KST boundary or a NULL-handling difference would silently change admin numbers, which the project treats as a judging risk (AGENTS.md guardrails).
findings.proposal: Add a CI job with `services: postgres` (or the supabase/postgres image) that applies RESET_AND_SETUP.sql, seeds fixtures (KST-midnight edges, simulate-peak same-timestamp ties, null levels, legacy score_breakdown, anonymous users) and asserts RPC output equals the existing Python aggregators, which are kept as oracles in tests. Run it with a TEST_DATABASE_URL env var and keep the default pytest run network-free per the current convention.
findings.makes_unnecessary: Hand-written 'this SQL must equal that Python' comments as the only guard; the ad-hoc WSL harnesses used for one-off validation.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: None to production. CI time grows by about 1 minute.

findings.title: Merchant /stats silently truncates at 1000 rows and pulls rows just to count them; the index it needs is missing
findings.evidence: merchant.py:129-156 makes three single-shot queries with `.limit(5000)` (user_coupons, congestion_logs user_report, recommendations by recommended_facility_id). PostgREST caps each response at 1000 rows, the same silent-truncation bug fixed elsewhere (admin.py:44-58, impact.py:67-70). The code then only does len() and sum() (161-173). audit:Web client data fetching (apps.subsystem: Web client data fetching (apps/web): lib/api-client.ts, app/main/page.tsx map load and fallback, lib/useCongestionAlerts.ts, lib/congestionEstimate.ts, lib/account.tsx, app/course, app/waiting, app/explore/recommend, admin dashboard fan-out
audit:Web client data fetching (apps.summary:
The client causes much of the load that the server-side patches (heavy-admin gate, RSS precheck, malloc_trim, per-request connections) are trying to absorb. The main problem is on the core map, which uses four sources for the same facility list: GET /infrastructures with a 4 s timeout, a Supabase-direct fallback, a 24 h localStorage copy, and a separate estimates poll. The race is built so that a slow API costs twice: the server keeps computing after the client times out, and the client then fetches from Supabase as well. The fallback that often wins is also wrong. Supabase caps every read at 1000 rows (core/supabase.py:365), and the measured map has 1682 facilities, so more than 40% of pins drop. The fallback also skips the is_active filter, and the result is cached for 24 h.

Other hotspots:
- **Prefetch on /main.** It fires 4 by-type calls plus a course build for every new session. The server cache is keyed per user, so this warms nothing for anyone else. It also inserts 32 recommendation rows that were never shown, which dilutes the admin accept-rate KPI.
- **/waiting forecast curve.** It makes 6 sequential /area-demand/forecast calls at about 3 s each, for a fixed location.
- **Stacked retries.** Retry layers at several levels re-run heavy, uncached POSTs after client timeouts, while the first run is still executing on the server.
- **Admin polling.** Two heavy admin GETs are polled every 30 s and 60 s even when the tab is hidden.
- **Tab focus.** Supabase auth-js 2.110.1 emits SIGNED_IN on every hidden-to-visible change, which refires /account/me and saved-list sync.
- **CORS preflight.** Every call adds a preflight to Render Oregon, the default region because render.yaml sets none.

**Proposed client side of a snapshot architecture**

1. **Facility snapshot (changes at most daily).**
   - Endpoints: `GET /api/v1/map/manifest` (about 200 B) and an immutable, content-hashed `GET /api/v1/map/facilities/{v}` served as pre-serialized bytes. It can later move to a Supabase Storage public bucket on the Seoul CDN.
   - Shape: one canonical key format, no keysToCamel. It carries only map, filter and search fields, including a precomputed search haystack. Overview, i18n text and the gallery go in a lazily loaded detail chunk.
   - Size: a synthetic benchmark with realistic Korean text gives about 330 KB raw, 105 KB gzip and 83 KB brotli, and parses in 0.36 ms. The current payload is 1.37 MB raw and 318 KB gzip.
   - Client: a new module `lib/mapData.ts`. It reads IndexedDB first (application-level stale-while-revalidate that works on every browser), revalidates the manifest, fetches the hashed file only when the version changes, and shares one in-flight promise across all consumers.
2. **Live layer (changes every 10 minutes and on reports).** One sparse `GET /api/v1/map/live`, with columns aligned to the snapshot version: measured level, timestamp, isCurrent flag, source, estimate columns and availability. It returns a weak ETag and is fetched with `cache: 'no-cache'`, so the browser sends If-None-Match itself and a 304 costs nothing. Clients poll it only while the tab is visible.
3. **Shared single-shot endpoints.**
   - `/area-demand/curve` for the 6-hour forecast.
   - `/recommendations/board` for the 4 waiting-board types in one request.
   - `/admin/dashboard/bundle` for the admin dashboard.

**What gets deleted once this lands:**
- The 4000 ms race and the whole Supabase fallback in main/page.tsx (575-743).
- The fallback mirror `measurementIsCurrentFallback` and its constants (congestionEstimate.ts 192-228), plus the backend parity test that exists only for it.
- The 24 h localStorage cache and `revalidateIsCurrent`.
- The separate estimates poll and the /freshness call with its Supabase fallback on /main and in DataFreshnessBadge.
- useCongestionAlerts polling the full /infrastructures.
- About 20 snake_case/camelCase double reads (`a ?? b`), which already caused a real search bug (placeSearch.ts:24-28).
- The prefetch, the per-page retry wrappers, and the loops in the waiting board and forecast curve.

**Rollout, stability first:**
- **Phase 0 (small, client only, safe before judging):** delete the prefetch, pause polling on hidden tabs, stop retrying after client timeouts, ignore same-uid SIGNED_IN events, fix the forecast step that always gets a 422, and optionally hotfix the fallback with pagination and is_active.
- **Phase 1:** add the new server endpoints. They are additive, so the OpenAPI snapshot grows but /infrastructures stays unchanged for bundles already deployed.
- **Phase 2:** switch the web app to `lib/mapData.ts` and delete the code listed above.
- **Phase 3:** add the board, curve and admin bundle endpoints.

No new i18n keys are needed: existing loading and error strings are reused, and the manifest's generatedAt feeds the existing sync label. Everything is a plain client fetch, so it fits the static export.

Sources:
- Render Blueprint default region is oregon: https://render.com/docs/blueprint-spec
- Render load balancers compress responses with Brotli and gzip: https://docs.render.com/web-services
- Cloudflare downgrades strong ETags to weak when it recompresses: https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/reference/etag-headers/
- Web Storage is limited to 5 MiB per origin: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Storage_API/Storage_quotas_and_eviction_criteria
- Starlette CORSMiddleware max_age default is 600, checked locally on starlette 1.3.1.

findings.title: Main map runs a 4 s race against the heaviest Render endpoint on every visit; losing the race doubles the load instead of saving it
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/main/page.tsx:575-743 — every mount first renders the localStorage copy (579-583). It then calls GET /api/v1/infrastructures with timeoutMs 4000 (597-605) and on any error runs two Supabase reads in parallel (651-668). The server handler apps/api/app/routers/infrastructures.py:370-440 has no cache and never checks for client disconnect: fetch_active_facilities select * paginated plus facility_source_refs (254-305), the latest_congestion RPC with every id, availability lookups, then 1682 pydantic models. The code's own comments admit the race is lost routinely: congestionEstimate.ts:200-203 ('프로덕션 TTFB 가 4.0~5.9초라 이 폴백이 드문 길이 아니다') and page.tsx:589-596. The estimates are also a separate 5-minute poll (780-807) because they could not ride on the slow endpoint (infrastructures.py:567-573).
findings.cost:
Per /main visit, measured facts: prod TTFB 2.7-4.2 s, 1.37 MB JSON (318 KB gzip), 2.0-2.7 s CPU and +17-25 MB transient heap per call locally. On the 0.5 CPU / 512 MB instance, every concurrent map open is a heap spike close to the OOM pattern.

When the 4 s timeout fires, the server still finishes the whole response, which is pure waste. The browser then also pulls about 1000 facility rows plus up to 1000 log rows (about 1.1 MB) from Supabase. Slower servers therefore trigger more double work, which is positive feedback under load.

Client side, from a Node benchmark on a 1.9 MB synthetic payload: JSON.parse 2.2 ms, keysToCamel 12.2 ms, cache JSON.stringify 4.9 ms. That is about 20 ms on desktop; a 4-5x slowdown for a mid-range phone is estimated, not measured.
findings.proposal:
Replace the race with two layers, each with one source of truth.

(1) Facility snapshot, which changes at most daily:
- `GET /api/v1/map/manifest` → `{v, count, generatedAt, tourapiSyncAt}` (about 200 B, `Cache-Control: no-cache`).
- `GET /api/v1/map/facilities/{v}` → pre-serialized, pre-compressed bytes built once per version and kept in memory, with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`.
- `v` is a hash of max(facilities.updated_at), count and the source_refs version. Bump it on ingest and on admin facility writes.
- Canonical compact shape: id, name, type, lat/lng as integer micro-degrees, capacity, a flags bitfield (barrier_free, parking, pet, indoor), cuisine and category, operating hours, rest_date_raw, menus, address, image_url, kakao url/id, contentid/contenttypeid, a precomputed search haystack, and a detail-chunk pointer.
- Overview, overview_i18n, gallery, homepage and phone go in `/map/facilities/{v}/detail`, loaded at idle or when a card opens.
- Benchmark with random Korean text: about 330 KB raw, 105 KB gzip, 83 KB brotli, 0.36 ms JSON.parse.
- Later, the same files can be uploaded by the ingest job to a Supabase Storage public bucket (Seoul CDN), which removes the endpoint from Render entirely. That step needs a person to create the bucket, so it goes on the HANDOVER 사람 작업 list.

(2) Live layer: `GET /api/v1/map/live` → `{snapshotV, observedAt, measured: {idx[], level[], ts[], isCurrent[], source[]}, estimate: {idx[], level[], parking[], tourism[], lotCount[], nearestLotM[], calibrated[]}, availability: [...]}`.
- It is sparse (only facilities that have data) and indexed by position in the snapshot. About 5 KB raw and 1.5 KB gzip for the measured part in the benchmark; the estimate columns stay a few KB because they are numeric.
- The server sets a weak ETag.
- The client fetches with `cache: 'no-cache'` and without auth or Content-Type headers, so it is a CORS simple request and the browser adds If-None-Match itself; a 304 costs about nothing.
- Poll every 5 minutes only while `document.visibilityState === 'visible'`.

Client module `lib/mapData.ts`:
- One module-level in-flight promise shared by /main, /saved, /mypage alerts and admin/infrastructure.
- Reads IndexedDB `{v, bytes}` first and renders it immediately (application-level stale-while-revalidate, portable to Safari).
- Then revalidates the manifest and fetches `/facilities/{v}` only if `v` changed; the browser HTTP cache also holds the immutable file.
- Writes back to IndexedDB and optionally notifies other tabs over BroadcastChannel.
- Exposes `useFacilities()` and `useLiveLayer()`; the map merges the two when drawing, as it already does for estimateById.
- No timeouts and no fallback are needed: first paint comes from IndexedDB or a small download, and if the network fails the stored snapshot remains correct.
findings.makes_unnecessary:
- main/page.tsx 211-243 (the 1.5M-character localStorage cache), 574-743 (API race and Supabase fallback), 745-775 (/freshness plus the Supabase updated_at fallback; the manifest carries tourapiSyncAt), 777-807 (separate estimates poll)
- congestionEstimate.ts 192-228 (measurementIsCurrentFallback, TRUSTED_EVIDENCE_TIERS, MEASUREMENT_NOW_WINDOW_MS) and 230-247 (revalidateIsCurrent exists only for the 24 h cache)
- apps/api/tests/services/test_congestion_estimate_evidence.py parity test (about 406-420)
- The 4000 ms special case
- The web's dependence on /infrastructures, which can be frozen for old bundles and removed after a transition window
- /warmup's facility-cache warming for the map path
- Most of the reason the server-side heavy-GET mitigations exist for tourist traffic
findings.stability_risk_of_change:
Medium.
- New additive endpoints; the OpenAPI snapshot changes but only by addition. Keep /infrastructures unchanged for bundles already deployed on Vercel.
- Risks: forgetting to bump the version on admin facility writes (mitigate by deriving `v` from max(updated_at) and count on each manifest request, cached for 60 s); IndexedDB being unavailable in private mode (fall back to memory only); ETag handling through Render's Cloudflare, where Cloudflare weakens strong ETags when recompressing, but weak ETags still work for If-None-Match; the e2e stub in e2e/voice-controls.spec.ts:43 and source-regex wiring tests must be updated.
- No SPOT or i18n impact. Everything is a client-side fetch, so the static export is preserved.

- `congestion_logs ... .limit(3000)`

findings.title: prefetchDemoHotPaths fires 4 engine by-type runs and a course build for every new session; the cache it 'warms' is per user, and it writes phantom recommendation rows
findings.evidence:
- apps/web/lib/api-client.ts:123-159: for each of 4 types, recommendByType(limit 8, 45 s), then POST /courses/plan (60 s). Once per sessionStorage session, fired from main/page.tsx:867-884 4 s after mount.
- The server cache key includes user_id (apps/api/app/routers/recommendations.py:910-919), so no other visitor benefits.
- Every by-type computation persists each returned item to `recommendations` (recommendations.py:1078-1128: '각 노출을 recommendations에 저장'), even though nothing was shown.
- The admin KPI computes the accept rate as accepted/total over those rows (app/admin/dashboard/page.tsx:510-531).
- The course path is 43 s cold (09-21) and 23 s on 09-26; recommendations.py:886-888 notes one by-type is '콜드 20초' and that overlapping runs starve the health check.
findings.cost:
Per new visitor on 0.5 CPU, in the cold case: 4 by-type pipelines (up to about 20 s each) plus 1 course build (23-43 s), roughly 1-2 CPU-minutes. That is issued whether or not the user ever opens /waiting or /course.

With 3 judges opening /main within minutes of each other, that is 15 heavy engine runs queued behind their own map loads. This is exactly the overlap that caused health-check restarts.

It also inserts 32 never-displayed recommendation rows per session (4 × limit 8), inflating the accept-rate denominator the admin dashboard shows to judges. That is a data-honesty risk.
findings.proposal:
Delete prefetchDemoHotPaths and its effect.

If instant /waiting is still wanted, make the expensive shared part user-independent:

- The admin dashboard withColdStartRetry does 3 attempts at 0 s / 1 s / 3.5 s (app/admin/dashboard/page.tsx:450-467) on heavy admin GETs with a 25 s timeout (lib/admin-api.ts:37). The server queues those behind a gate of 2 (apps/api/app/core/memory_guard.py:50).
- Course plan retries on 503/429 (app/course/page.tsx:482-486).
- The waiting board has two retry passes (waiting/page.tsx:454-463, 577-581).
- api-client retries every non-FormData request, POSTs included, once on a TypeError (api-client.ts:227-278). The comment assumes 'server not reached', but edge-generated 502/503/524 responses without CORS headers (Render restarting or OOM) also surface as a TypeError after the origin may already have executed part of the request.
findings.cost:
In exactly the overload windows the retries are meant to cover, each user action turns into 2-5 full engine runs (0.5-20 s each). The server cannot cancel, because to_thread work continues after disconnect.

Non-idempotent POSTs create duplicate recommendation rows. HANDOVER 09-26 already records duplicate POSTs from the retry transport as a known issue.

Admin: 7 heavy GETs × up to 3 attempts queued behind a gate of 2 means a timeout at 25 s puts another copy in the queue, stretching the OOM-prone window instead of shrinking it.
findings.proposal:
Centralize one retry policy in `request()` and delete every page-level retry.
1. Automatic retry only for GET, and only on (a) a TypeError before any response, (b) 503/429 honoring `Retry-After` (cap 1 retry, jittered).
2. Never auto-retry after a client-side timeout. The server is still working; re-issuing duplicates the work.
3. For heavy POSTs (recommendations, by-type, courses/plan, board), send an `X-Request-Id` generated once per user intent and reused on any manual 'retry' tap. The server uses it as a single-flight key: the existing ResponseCache in app/core/response_cache.py already supports join-in-flight, keyed here by the request id, so a retry joins the running computation instead of starting another and never persists twice.
4. Pass AbortSignal everywhere (the course page does not), so late responses are ignored cheaply.
5. Admin: one attempt plus a visible 'retry' button (the lib/adminApiFailure.ts messaging already exists); drop withColdStartRetry.

audit:Recommendation + course comput.summary:
Bottom line: the "one Dijkstra per candidate pair" suspicion is wrong. Routes are already batched: 1 search per request for /recommendations and /by-type (recommendations.py:544, 983), 1 per slot in courses (courses.py:848), and score.py gets travel overrides from every caller. The real problem is the shape of the pipeline. Each request fans out one async task per candidate (hundreds for by-type; cafes and restaurants are 1,567 of 1,669 active places, docs/CONGESTION_DATA.md:424). Each task makes its own trips to the thread pool, mostly into the shared 16-thread I/O pool (main.py:39): the sklearn predict up to 3 times, one area-demand RPC per 100 m grid cell, a backtest, and threading.Event waits. Meanwhile static data is recomputed on every request: facility-to-node snapping, full-graph Dijkstra, a deepcopy of all facility rows, opening-hours regex, and sklearn one-hot encoding. That pool flooding is the mechanism behind the /account/me timeouts and health-check starvation, and the area-demand grid cache (44-86 MB) is the largest movable chunk of the 512 MB budget.

Measured locally (Windows desktop, py3.11, real repo graph: 28,832 nodes / 62,304 edges, 9 components, largest 98.8%):
- Current dict graph: 0.06 s load (0.57 s under tracemalloc), +29.0 MB private (16.7 MB live objects, 27.4 MB peak).
- scipy CSR + cKDTree built offline as .npz: 0.011 s load, +3.2 MB. The stdlib array() binary is 0.36 MB gzipped, 0.78 MB raw, and loads in 3.4 ms.
- Snapping costs 373-475 us per point today, vs 18 us with a ring grid and 7 us with cKDTree.
- Whenever any target snaps into one of the 8 small components, the current Dijkstra settles all 28,489 nodes (17-22 ms). With 300 candidates that happens on about 97% of by-type requests. A search bounded by a limit plus a component pre-check settles 2,468 nodes in 1.4 ms; csgraph with limit takes 0.29 ms.
- End-to-end route stage for by-type: 135 ms (300 candidates) and 247 ms (600) today, vs 0.5-0.6 ms (CSR) or about 2 ms (stdlib bounded). About 90% of the current cost is snapping.
- csgraph releases the GIL: the main thread ran at 108% of its solo rate, vs 64% while pure-Python Dijkstra ran in a worker.
- However, importing numpy + scipy.sparse + csgraph adds about 34 MB working set when sklearn is not already loaded, which cancels the saving. So the default recommendation is stdlib arrays; switch to csgraph only if numpy is resident anyway.
- sklearn predict takes 360 us per call vs 0.06 us for a 672-cell table. Importing sklearn Ridge + OneHot adds 54 MB working set.
- A facility x facility walking matrix (1682^2) is feasible (dense uint16 5.7 MB; pairs within 2 km 11.9% = 1.3 MB sparse; 0.4 s to build offline with csgraph) but unnecessary. Slot 1 starts at an arbitrary user position, and one bounded search per slot costs 1-2 ms. Precompute facility-to-node snaps instead.

Scripts are in the scratchpad (bench_graph.py, bench_graph2.py, bench_predict.py). Sources: scipy csgraph.dijkstra docs (limit returns inf for nodes beyond it, the same value as "not connected") https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.csgraph.dijkstra.html ; OpenBLAS ignores cgroup CPU limits https://github.com/OpenMathLib/OpenBLAS/issues/6059 and https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/35017.

findings.title: Per-candidate async fan-out floods the shared 16-thread I/O executor (scoring loop: predict hop + area-demand RPC + backtest + Event waits per candidate)
findings.evidence: recommendations.py:640-642 and 1054 run asyncio.gather over ALL eligible candidates (the 2 km box in by-type, recommendations.py:962-975). For each candidate, score.py:111-116 always makes an asyncio.to_thread(predict_congestion_detailed) call, even with no model, and score.py:119 calls get_area_demand_signal. That function does area_demand_service.py:374-389 (a gather plus the history path), then area_demand_forecast_service.py:554 (one to_thread RPC per uncached 100 m grid; only a per-grid lock at :573, no global cap), then :728 (to_thread backtest per candidate), which can block a pool thread in running.wait() at :978. recommendations.py:376-378 adds another predict hop, and :1063/:316-333 run the area-demand work again for the top-N. Only courses prefetch, with a semaphore of 6 (courses.py:695-704, forecast_service.py:650-693); /by-type and /recommendations do not. All of this shares the default pool (main.py:39 _IO_EXECUTOR_MAX_WORKERS=16, installed at main.py:49-62) with every other request's Supabase calls and DNS lookups (main.py:30-38 comments). The points cache holds 96 grids (forecast_service.py:137), fewer than the distinct grids in a 2 km by-type box, so it thrashes within a single request.
findings.cost: 300 candidates means at least 300 pool jobs: 9 ms of event-loop and pool overhead for no-op hops, 160 ms if the sklearn model is active (bench_predict.py). On top of that, one RPC per uncached grid at 0.5-1.2 s each (forecast_service.py:135) goes through 16 FIFO threads. For example, 100 grid misses is about 5-8 s during which every other request's to_thread I/O (/account/me, JWKS, facility lookups) waits in the queue. That is the documented 09-26 bounce ('course compute 23 s -> /account/me 10 s timeout', HANDOVER.md:237) and the health-starvation restarts. The demo assumed-time presets force the history path for every candidate, and the web client prefetches exactly those requests (web lib/api-client.ts:123-157).
findings.proposal:
Replace per-candidate coroutines with a two-phase 'gather-then-compute' candidate pipeline in one service module (services/spot/pipeline.py), not in routers.
- Phase A, bulk I/O, a fixed handful of awaits per request regardless of candidate count: the facility snapshot (memory), the latest-congestion RPC (1 call), availability and timesales (whole active set, see the availability/timesale finding), the area-demand lookup table (see the area-demand finding), the prediction table (see the predict finding), and the user vector.
- Phase B: one synchronous pure-CPU function scores all candidates, run once (inline if under ~5 ms, else one job on a dedicated 1-thread CPU executor). It calls a sync twin of calculate_spot_score whose arithmetic is moved verbatim from score.py:57-296, with the prefetched inputs passed as overrides. score.py already has this pattern with travel_time_override. calculate_spot_score stays as a thin async wrapper, so the weight-parity test and the SPOT constants are untouched.
- Courses reuse the same pipeline per slot.
- The helpers courses.py imports from routers (courses.py:62-70: build_candidate_evidence, fetch_all_facilities, fetch_congestion_map, the infrastructures model) move into the service, which removes 3 of the router-layer violations listed in the G0-G3 plan.
findings.makes_unnecessary: Per-candidate to_thread in score.py:111 and courses.py:310. prefetch_area_demand_points and its semaphore. _points_locks and _quality_inflight single-flight plus the threading.Event waits (forecast_service.py:141, 205-214, 965-1006). Most of the reason the by-type and course ResponseCaches exist. The warmup area_demand step (warmup.py:169). The client prefetchDemoHotPaths. A good part of the rationale for the 1 ms GIL switch interval (main.py:41-46).
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Medium. score.py is a caution zone. The sync twin must be byte-for-byte the same arithmetic; lock it with the existing golden scores (scripts/recommendation_quality.py) and the ranking tests, and diff-compare old vs new on recorded candidate sets. Removing per-candidate try/gather changes the partial-failure semantics: keep courses.py:863-882 'drop a failed candidate, 503 only if all fail' by catching per candidate inside Phase B.

findings.title: Area-demand signal is recomputed per candidate at request time; it should be a table precomputed at the 10-minute collect
findings.evidence: score.py:119 calls area_demand_service.get_area_demand_signal for every candidate. The history path (area_demand_service.py:384-389) issues one RPC per 100 m grid that returns the full 56-day series of 4,172-8,064 points (forecast_service.py:540-555), caches up to 96 grids at 0.46-0.9 MB each (forecast_service.py:129-138; the comment there says 256 grids was 118 MB and a main OOM driver), and runs a 28-day backtest per grid (forecast_service.py:775-854). The backtest cache key includes points[-1].observed_at (forecast_service.py:959-964), so every 10-minute snapshot invalidates every grid's quality result despite the 30-minute TTL. Yet the whole information content is tiny: Gyeongju has 4 real-time ITS lots, 3 near Hwangnidan-gil (docs/CONGESTION_ENGINE_PLAN.md:256). Every grid series is sum(w_l*occ_l,t)/sum(w_l) over at most 4 lots (aggregate_nearby_points, forecast_service.py:249-280).
findings.cost: Memory: 44-86 MB for the grid cache (HANDOVER's pending 'GridSeries -74MB'). Latency: course cold path of 43 s (09-21) and 23 s (09-26); by-type with assumed-time presets 20 s cold (recommendations.py:884-888). Each uncached grid is a 0.5-1.2 s RPC plus a backtest, and courses' 36-54 pool coordinates run at 6 concurrent. The quality cache is effectively reset every 10 minutes.
findings.makes_unnecessary: The area_demand_points_near RPC in the request path, _points_cache, _series_indexes, the _points_locks and intern tables (forecast_service.py:66-99, 112-189), _quality_cache and its inflight machinery, _raw_cache fallback (forecast_service.py:102-110, 604-647, already marked 'delete after migration'), prefetch_area_demand_points, warmup's area_demand step, and _attach_delayed_area_actions' second round of RPCs.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Medium. This overlaps the area-demand subsystem. The RPC is currently the canonical path (forecast_service.py:237-240), so the in-process aggregation must be proven equal against it with the existing contract tests. The behaviour must stay honest when the collect is late: fall back to 'no signal' (None), never to a stale value presented as a forecast.

findings.title: Walking graph: 29 MB of dicts, and every request re-snaps all candidates and usually explores the whole graph
findings.evidence: travel.py:55-84 builds dict[int, tuple] coordinates, dict[int, list[tuple]] adjacency and a spatial dict from gz JSON. travel.py:162-165 snaps every destination on every request with _nearest_node (travel.py:87-111: haversine over all nodes in a 5x5 grid of 0.002-degree cells). travel.py:114-133 keeps searching until all targets are found, so one target snapped into any of the 8 small components (343 nodes) forces exploration of the whole 28,489-node component. There is no distance limit, even though callers discard routes longer than max_walk_minutes (recommendations.py:551, 995). Callers: recommendations.py:544 and 983 (every candidate), courses.py:848 (12 per slot).
findings.cost:
Measured locally with the real graph.
- Load: 0.06 s, +29.0 MB private (16.7 MB live objects, 27.4 MB transient peak).
- Snapping: 373-475 us per point. For 300 or 600 by-type candidates that is 111-224 ms of GIL-holding CPU per request.
- Dijkstra: settles 28,489 nodes (17-22 ms) in by-type almost always. With 300 targets, P(at least one in a small component) is about 97%; my 12-target course sample hit it too.
- End to end: by-type 135 ms (300) and 247 ms (600) on the desktop. Expect roughly 4-8x that on Render's 0.5 CPU, while starving the loop (the main thread ran at 64% of its solo rate).
findings.proposal:
Precompute offline in scripts/build_walking_graph.py, which already exists. Emit a compact binary: int32 microdegree coordinates, CSR int32 indptr and indices, uint16 metres (max edge is 717 m), uint16 component id, and a cell-sorted spatial index. That is 0.78 MB raw, 0.36 MB gzipped, 3.4 ms to load with array.frombytes, and no new dependency.
At facility-snapshot build, compute each facility's (node, snap_m, component) once: 18 us each with a ring grid, and the result matches the current snap on 599 of 600 points.
Per request, snap only the origin, drop targets in other components up front (identical result: they fall back to the estimate anyway), and run a Dijkstra bounded by limit = max_walk_m, or about 1.5x the course haversine cap. That settles about 2,468 nodes in 1.4 ms.
Important: a target beyond the limit must be reported as 'too far', not as unreachable. Otherwise the current fallback at travel.py:172-174 would promote it to an estimated route that passes the walking filter. The same trap applies to scipy's limit, which returns inf for such nodes.
If numpy/scipy are resident anyway (an active sklearn model), csgraph.dijkstra(indices=src, limit=L) takes 0.29 ms and releases the GIL (108% main-thread rate). Do not import scipy only for this: numpy + scipy.sparse + csgraph costs +34 MB working set, more than the 26 MB saved.
Do not build a facility x facility matrix: it is feasible (1.3 MB sparse within 2 km, 0.4 s to build) but redundant with the 1-2 ms bounded search, and it cannot serve slot 1, which starts from an arbitrary origin.
findings.makes_unnecessary: _graph_lock plus the cold-load stampede reasoning (travel.py:17-20), the warmup walking_graph step (warmup.py:164), most of the justification for asyncio.to_thread in get_walking_routes (travel.py:136-147; keep it or run inline, since about 2 ms no longer matters), and the gz JSON parse at boot.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low to medium. Distances are bit-identical for reachable targets within the limit (mismatch 0 in all scenarios). tests/services/test_walking_graph.py monkeypatches _graph_cache and the dict shape, so those tests need a rewrite. Keep the contract tests (the 196 m real-graph route, fallback outside the snap range, loop not blocked). Get the too-far vs unreachable semantics right as described above.

findings.title: sklearn predict called up to 3x per candidate via to_thread, although the model is a 672-cell additive table; sklearn/OpenBLAS in the API is a latent memory and thread hazard
findings.evidence: scripts/train.py:68-74 fits Ridge on a one-hot of (type, hour, dow), so the prediction is fully determined by 4x24x7 = 672 cells. predict_service.py:208-218 runs encoder.transform plus model.predict on every call. Per course candidate the same (type, arrival hour, dow) is predicted 3 times: courses.py:310-312, score.py:111-116, and recommendations.py:376-378 when there are no logs. safety.py:67-68 calls it synchronously ON the event loop, twice per facility with logs. predict.py:246 and 336-347 make 24 sequential to_thread calls per /predict/day. _load_artifact unpickles sklearn objects (predict_service.py:94-117). Dockerfile sets no OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS.
findings.cost: 360 us per call vs 0.06 us for a table lookup; 300 candidates through gather take 160 ms vs 9 ms (bench_predict.py). Only paid once a model passes the promotion gates, but then it is also a +54 MB working-set sklearn import (measured). Without OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, numpy committed +446 MB private on Windows, and on Linux containers OpenBLAS sizes its thread pool to the host's cores, not the 0.5 CPU quota (sources cited in the summary). In other words, activating a model could itself trigger an OOM or CPU thrash on the 512 MB instance.
findings.proposal:
Short term: when a model version activates, build TABLE[(type, hour, dow)] once, predicting per cell so the floats are identical. Batch predict differed in the last bits in 2 of 672 cells, so either build per cell (672 x 360 us = 0.24 s once per version) or accept a ~1e-16 difference. Cells outside the encoder categories map to None, same as today. predict_congestion becomes a dict lookup with no to_thread at any call site.
Offline, the better design: train.py exports the 672 floats (plus categories) into the artifact or model_registry as JSON, and the API loads a list. The API then never imports numpy, scipy or sklearn and never runs pickle.load.
Add ENV OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 and OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 to the Dockerfile regardless.
findings.makes_unnecessary: Every asyncio.to_thread(predict_*) (courses.py:310, score.py:111, recommendations.py:376, predict.py:130-133, 246, 336, 347), the duplicate predictions per candidate, the sklearn/pickle import in the API process, and the sha256+pickle validation surface (keep the hash check for the JSON).
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low. The contract is identical when built per cell. tests/services/test_predict_service.py asserts None for unseen combinations, which the table preserves. The registry and artifact format changes only on the training side, and a version bump is needed.

findings.title: Availability and timesale overlays query hundreds of ids in 150-id IN-list chunks per request, for tables whose active sets are tiny
findings.evidence: availability_service.py:44-100 splits into 150-id chunks run in parallel. Its comment documents the history: a 60 KB URL caused a Cloudflare 520 after about 9 s, which silently emptied the evidence. merchant_boost.py:57-100 fetches timesales in 150-id chunks sequentially. /by-type fetches availability for ALL facility types in the 2 km box (recommendations.py:965 -> fetch_all_facilities with_availability=True, :295-303) and only then filters to one type (:969-975). /recommendations does the same before filtering by context (:511-533).
findings.cost: Per request: ceil(N_box/150) availability calls (up to 11 for all facilities, recommendations.py:260-261) plus ceil(N_candidates/150) sequential timesale calls. Each is a pool job and one of the Supabase HTTP/1.1 exclusive connections (core/supabase.py). Most of the availability rows fetched in by-type belong to types that are thrown away. Chunking and silent-empty behaviour are an ongoing correctness hazard.
findings.proposal:
Query the whole active set, never an IN-list:
- availability: SELECT ... FROM facility_availability_reports WHERE evidence_tier='corroborated' AND expires_at > now() ORDER BY reported_at DESC
- timesales: SELECT ... FROM merchant_timesales WHERE canceled_at IS NULL AND now() BETWEEN starts_at AND ends_at
Both results are small (corroborated reports expire in 30-60 minutes; active timesales are a handful). Keep each in one shared 30 s single-flight cache and join per request with a dict lookup. Also filter by type and context BEFORE any per-facility work in by-type and /recommendations.
findings.makes_unnecessary: _AVAILABILITY_ID_CHUNK/_TIMESALE_ID_CHUNK chunking, the per-chunk failure isolation, the with_availability/copy_rows flags on fetch_all_facilities, and courses' separate pool-only availability fetch (courses.py:667-676, 695-697).
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low. The semantics are identical: newest unexpired corroborated report per facility, and the maximum active timesale rate. Freshness drops by at most 30 s from the cache, which is inside the documented 30/60-minute evidence windows. The judge demo flow (a merchant broadcast shows up 'within the same demo') still holds if the cache is invalidated on merchant writes.

findings.title: Response caches are keyed per user, so every new user pays the full non-personal pipeline; the client prefetch and warmup patch around it
findings.evidence: by-type cache key starts with user_id (recommendations.py:910-919), and so does the course key (courses.py:440-448). ResponseCache holds 64 entries with a 180 s TTL and deep-copies on store and read (response_cache.py:17-22, 49-52). Yet everything expensive is user-independent: routes from the origin cell, congestion evidence, area demand, arrival eligibility, and predictions. Only W1 (an 8-dim cosine plus the cuisine intent match, preference.py:84-127) and the user vector are personal. Patches that exist because of this: web prefetchDemoHotPaths fires 4 by-type calls and 1 course call per session (api-client.ts:123-157), warmBackend and /warmup (warmup.py:1-19, 45 s budget), and the response caches themselves.
findings.cost: The first request of each judge or user is the cold 20 s (by-type) or 23-43 s (course) path (recommendations.py:884-888, warmup.py:5-6). Each cold user replays hundreds of candidate evaluations that differ from another user's only in the W1 term.
findings.proposal: Once the fan-out, area-demand, walking-graph and predict findings make the pipeline a few ms of CPU, split the cache along the real dependency line. Cache a shared 'candidate context' keyed by (origin 100 m cell, facility type or pool, context signature, 10-minute time bucket). It holds per-candidate non-personal inputs: route, evidence, predicted and area inputs, and the eligibility tier. The personal pass runs the W1 cosine for each candidate plus the score formula, which takes microseconds. The ranking formula is unchanged.
findings.makes_unnecessary: prefetchDemoHotPaths (web), most of /warmup and the lifespan warmup of area context, and per-user response-cache deep copies. For by-type you may keep the ResponseCache only for recommendation_id stability.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Medium. Cache-key completeness is the correctness risk; the current keys document every field that can change the answer, and the new key must too. Merchant seat broadcasts must invalidate the shared context for that facility.

findings.title: All facility rows are deep-copied per request on the event loop, and again on every cache store
findings.evidence: fetch_all_facilities defaults to copy_rows=True (recommendations.py:245-281). /recommendations (:511) and /by-type (:965) take that default, so get_facilities_cached(isolate=True) runs copy.deepcopy over every cached row (facility_cache.py:97-98), plus once more on reload (facility_cache.py:33). The copy is redundant: downstream code never mutates shared rows in place. attach_availability_evidence returns {**f} copies (availability_service.py:101-111), apply_merchant_boosts copies with dict(f) (merchant_boost.py:51), score.py copies features (score.py:60), and the one in-place mutator, attach_related_destination_priors (tourism_related_service.py:78-84), runs on those shallow copies.
findings.cost: 16 ms desktop per 1,682 synthetic rows (1.65 KB JSON per row, shaped like select *) and about 1.5 MB transient, synchronous on the event loop. Roughly 60-100 ms of loop stall per request on 0.5 CPU.
findings.proposal: Treat the facility list as an immutable snapshot built once per reload: a tuple of rows, with nested features frozen or never handed out mutable. Build the derived per-facility precomputes at the same time: graph snap, area grid key and weights, parsed opening hours, type code. Request code works only on shallow overlays, which it already does. This snapshot is the natural single owner that replaces the 4 independent facility caches noted in the brief.
findings.makes_unnecessary: The copy_rows/isolate flags and their comments (recommendations.py:255-259, facility_cache.py:89-98), the deepcopy on store, and courses' pool deepcopy (courses.py:652-655).
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low to medium. Needs a guard test that fails if any request path mutates a snapshot row. Freezing with MappingProxyType in tests catches it cheaply.

findings.title: Top-N recommendations persisted as N separate INSERT round trips per request, each storing the breakdown twice
findings.evidence: /recommendations runs asyncio.gather(_persist(item) for the top 5) (recommendations.py:676-750), each an asyncio.to_thread single-row insert, with a legacy retry at :736-743. /by-type does the same for limit rows, up to 20 (recommendations.py:1082-1129). Each row stores score_breakdown and a recommendation_snapshot that contains the same breakdown again (:685, :727-729; :1088, :1120-1121).
findings.cost: 5-20 pool jobs and HTTP round trips per recommendation request, on the latency-critical path, plus 2x breakdown JSON written per row. A partial failure degrades to 'mock-rec-id' (:755-761).
findings.proposal: Generate uuid4 recommendation ids in the API and write all rows with one supabase insert([...]) call: one round trip, all-or-nothing. Store the breakdown once, in the snapshot (explain already falls back from snapshot to score_breakdown, recommendations.py:833-841), or keep score_breakdown and slim the snapshot. Optionally write after building the response, since the ids are already known.
findings.makes_unnecessary: The per-row gather with return_exceptions, the mock-rec-id index-alignment logic, and the legacy column retry once the migration is confirmed.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low. A schema and aggregation check is needed if any admin query reads score_breakdown. The ids stay UUIDs, so the web contract is unchanged.

findings.title: Industry baseline medians computed in Python from every trusted congestion_logs row
findings.evidence: spot/industry_baseline.py:106-118 pages through ALL trusted congestion_logs rows with an embedded facilities(type) join (fetch_all_rows, core/supabase.py:356-381) to produce 4 medians. The 1 h TTL and an asyncio lock (industry_baseline.py:121-155) sit inside the scoring path (score.py:181-182), so the first degraded_rules candidate after expiry blocks the rest of the request.
findings.cost: The table grows without bound: 2,705 rows at 09-07 (industry_baseline.py:108-109) and more every day. One multi-page fetch per hour lands on a user request. Low per-request cost but a latency cliff.
findings.proposal: Move the aggregation into SQL: an RPC or view with percentile_cont(0.5) GROUP BY type, filtered by the trusted tiers and the MIN_* sample rules, returning 4 rows. Better still, compute it in the weekly train job and store it next to the model table, so scoring reads 4 floats.
findings.makes_unnecessary: _median_congestion_by_type, the paginated fetch, and the lock and TTL in the request path.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low. The value must match the Python median (tests exist for _median_congestion_by_type).

findings.title: Opening hours regex-parsed on every call, 2-4 calls per candidate
findings.evidence: open_status_at_arrival re-parses operating_hours with re.search/re.findall on every call (travel_context.py:80-125). recommendation_eligibility_tier calls it twice per candidate (travel_context.py:153-169, via arrival_ineligibility_reason and directly). It is called again in persist and response (recommendations.py:687-690, 784-786) and per course evaluation (courses.py:415, 887).
findings.cost: Microseconds per call, since 96.55% of cafes and restaurants have no hours (CONGESTION_DATA.md:424). Roughly 10 ms per 600-candidate request; minor.
findings.proposal: Parse each facility's hours once, at facility-snapshot build (see the deep-copy finding), into a compact form: a closed-weekday bitmask plus minute ranges for weekday and weekend. open_status becomes arithmetic. Compute the tier once and reuse it for the response and persist steps.
findings.makes_unnecessary: Repeated regex compilation and matching, and the duplicate open_status calls.
findings.stability_risk_of_change: Low, with a golden test over all distinct operating_hours strings comparing old and new.

findings.title: Dead or redundant code in the compute path
findings.evidence: The routing branch at score.py:84-91 and its import at score.py:6 (get_travel_time_and_distance, travel.py:190-195) are unused in production: all 4 callers pass travel_time_override (courses.py:393, recommendations.py:621 and 1041, scripts/recommendation_quality.py:76). recommendations.py:203-210 is a pure pass-through wrapper. forecast_service.py:102-110 and 604-647 are the RPC-missing fallback, which its own comment marks for deletion once the migration is confirmed.
findings.cost: Maintenance risk rather than runtime: a future caller that omits the override silently gets a second route search and mislabelled travel_source='estimated' (see the comment at courses.py:388-392).
findings.proposal: Make the travel override required, as a keyword-only argument or by asserting it, in the sync score twin from the fan-out finding, and delete the in-score routing path. Remove the wrapper and the confirmed-dead fallback.
findings.makes_unnecessary: get_travel_time_and_distance and the score.py -> travel.py import coupling.

audit:Reference-data read path: faci.subsystem: Reference-data read path: facilities, facility_source_refs, latest congestion, availability evidence, timesales, congestion estimates, parking lots, tourism priors, and industry baselines.
